note: Context-fit rules used by the guided assessment. These are AI-authored editorial judgements about which tools serve which kind of work, and they are unreviewed. They deliberately live in content rather than code so a reviewer can audit them. Repository signals do not contribute to any rule here.

still_appropriate.sass: Still fine where it already exists. A working stylesheet is an asset; migrating it wholesale rarely pays for itself.
still_appropriate.bootstrap: Reasonable to keep on an existing internal or admin interface. Replacing it is a redesign, not an upgrade.
still_appropriate.npm: No reason to change package manager purely for its own sake on a codebase you are maintaining.

reconsider.gulp: The bundler now owns the dependency graph that Gulp used to orchestrate. Keeping it means maintaining a plugin chain that newer tooling makes unnecessary.
reconsider.grunt: Superseded by Gulp and then by bundlers. A Gruntfile is usually the oldest thing in a repository.
reconsider.jquery: Most of what it was used for is now native: querySelectorAll, classList, fetch. It is often the easiest dependency to remove outright.
reconsider.bower: Deprecated by its own maintainers and the registry is effectively frozen — no security advisories will reach you.
reconsider.angularjs: End of life since 2022 and receives no security patches. On anything handling user data this is a risk, not a preference.
reconsider.webpack: Still capable, but if the dev-server wait is part of your daily cost, that cost is now avoidable.

candidates.why: You are maintaining a build that predates bundlers owning the dependency graph. Vite is the smallest step that removes the plugin chain and the dev-server wait at the same time.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Your build depends on webpack-specific loaders or module federation with no Vite equivalent — check before committing to a migration.

candidates.why: You marked jQuery. htmx lets you keep server-rendered pages and drop the jQuery dependency without adopting a client-side framework — the smaller of the two available moves.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The application has genuinely rich client state — an editor, a canvas, real-time collaboration — in which case a framework is the right answer, not htmx.

candidates.why: Refactoring a codebase you did not write is exactly where types earn their cost — accurate rename and reference-finding across unfamiliar code.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The codebase is small enough to hold in your head, or the team will not invest in learning the type system and will reach for `any`.

candidates.why: On an older repository with a large dependency tree, the strict layout surfaces undeclared dependencies that npm silently tolerates — a common source of surprise during a migration.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Packages in your tree rely on a flat, permissive node_modules layout.

candidates.why: Legacy maintenance is mostly reading unfamiliar code and making mechanical changes across many files, which is the shape of work agentic tools handle best.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Your organisation cannot send source code to a third-party service.

still_appropriate.sass: Fine for content sites, though check how much of what you use is now native CSS.
still_appropriate.bootstrap: Defensible when you need a working layout faster than a distinctive one.
still_appropriate.tailwind: Works well here — content sites usually have few enough templates that utility classes stay manageable.

reconsider.nextjs: For a content site this is often more rendering machinery than the job needs.
reconsider.react: A content site rarely needs a client-side framework runtime shipped to every visitor.
reconsider.webpack: Heavier than a content build requires.

candidates.why: You build content sites. Astro ships zero JavaScript by default and lets you opt into interactivity per component — the inverse of the framework assumption, and the right default for content.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The site is really an application in disguise, with pervasive client state across most of the page.

candidates.why: Content sites have a small number of templates, so a fixed token scale gives you consistency without building a design system first.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Non-developers edit the templates without running the build, or the markup must stay framework-neutral for third parties.

candidates.why: For a simple new stack this is the least you can adopt and still get a fast modern build.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are using a framework that brings its own build and adding Vite separately would duplicate it.

candidates.why: Content work involves a lot of repetitive template and copy editing, which is where editor-integrated assistance pays off most directly.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are committed to an editor other than VS Code, or cannot send source to a third party.

still_appropriate.react: A reasonable default for application work, and the largest hiring pool.
still_appropriate.vite: The current default build for application work.
still_appropriate.typescript: Effectively expected on any application a team maintains.
still_appropriate.tailwind: Works well in component-based application code.

reconsider.jquery: In an application codebase this usually indicates a layer nobody has revisited.
reconsider.webpack: Capable, but the dev-server cost is now avoidable.
reconsider.styled-components: Runtime CSS-in-JS fits server rendering poorly and costs render performance.
reconsider.jest: If you already build with Vite, a second build configuration for tests is avoidable.

candidates.why: You build applications a team maintains. Types pay for themselves on refactoring and editor tooling long before they pay off on bug-catching.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The project is a prototype you expect to throw away.

candidates.why: You already build with Vite, so tests can share that configuration instead of maintaining a second one.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are on React Native, where Jest remains better supported.

candidates.why: Most application state turns out to be a cache of server data. Naming that distinction removes a lot of hand-written loading and refetch logic.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Your state is genuinely client-side — editor buffers, form drafts — or your framework already provides a data layer.

candidates.why: Application work is where end-to-end coverage matters most, and auto-waiting removes the flakiness that usually kills these suites.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You have no capacity to maintain an E2E suite — an ignored suite is worse than none.

candidates.why: Application changes usually span several files and need tests run between steps, which is the shape of task an agentic tool handles.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You cannot send source code to a third-party service.

still_appropriate.storybook: The right tool for this work — it is where a design system crosses a team boundary.
still_appropriate.sass: Mixins and compile-time logic are one of the few remaining cases with no native equivalent, and design systems are that case.
still_appropriate.typescript: Consumers of your components expect type definitions.
still_appropriate.figma: Where the tokens you are implementing usually originate.

reconsider.tailwind: Components consumed by other teams generally need to emit semantic, restyleable markup. Utility classes in a shared library push your styling decisions into their markup.
reconsider.bootstrap: A design system usually exists precisely because an off-the-shelf component set was not distinctive enough.
reconsider.styled-components: Runtime styling in a shared library imposes its cost on every consumer.

candidates.why: You build components other people consume. CSS Modules give you scoping while emitting ordinary, restyleable CSS — which matters when the consumer needs to override you.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You need a shared token scale supplied for you rather than authored, in which case a framework is the better fit.

candidates.why: Querying by accessible role is doubly useful in a component library: the tests survive refactors, and a component you cannot query by role is usually one a screen reader cannot navigate.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are testing genuinely internal logic, which belongs in plain unit tests.

candidates.why: Consumers of a component library expect type definitions; shipping without them pushes the cost onto every team that uses you.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You already ship types via JSDoc and the build cost is not worth changing.

candidates.why: Component libraries benefit from visual and interaction coverage across engines, since you cannot control which browser a consumer targets.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Your CI cannot run browser binaries.

reconsider.angularjs: End of life. Learning it now teaches you a framework you will only ever encounter in maintenance.
reconsider.bower: Deprecated. Any tutorial teaching it is at least eight years old, and so is everything else in it.
reconsider.grunt: Superseded twice over. Useful to recognise, not to learn.

candidates.why: You are building your foundation. Types are assumed by most current tutorials, libraries and job descriptions, so learning JavaScript and TypeScript together avoids relearning later.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are still getting comfortable with JavaScript itself — in that case types are a second thing to learn at the same time.

candidates.why: It is the current default build tool and requires almost no configuration, so you can learn it without learning build engineering first.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are following a course built around a different toolchain — fighting the course is not worth it.

candidates.why: Not because it is the best, but because it is the assumption most tutorials, libraries and job listings are written against — which makes everything else easier to read.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are drawn to a simpler model; Vue or Svelte are easier starting points and the concepts transfer.

candidates.why: Worth learning deliberately rather than by osmosis — including where it misleads you, which matters more while you are still building judgement.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are learning fundamentals and would accept generated code you cannot yet evaluate. That is the main trap.
